 1 I.        IDENTIFICATION


2    Q.       PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS FOR THE RECORD.

3    A.       My name is Larry Blank.        My business address is TAHOEconomics, LLC, 6061

4             Montgomery Road, Midlothian, TX 76065. My email address is LB@tahoeconomics.com.

5    Q.       WHERE ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 6   A.       I am the principal of TAHOEconomics, LLC (“Tahoe”), a Texas-registered consulting firm

7             I founded in August 1999 (originally in Nevada), specializing in most policy and

8             ratemaking facets of regulated utility industries. I am also a Professor of Economics in the

9             College of Business at New Mexico State University (“NMSU”). For the purposes of this

10            proceeding, I have been engaged through Tahoe. The expert opinions expressed herein are

11            my own, and nothing in this testimony necessarily reflects the opinions of NMSU.

12     Q.     PLEASE PROVIDE A BRIEF SUMMARY OF YOUR BACKGROUND AS IT IS

13            RELEVANT TO THIS TESTIMONY.

14     A.     I received a Ph.D. in Economics from The University of Tennessee in 1994, specializing

15            in Industrial Organization & Public Policy (including regulatory policy), Econometrics,

16            and Finance. I previously served as an Economist with the National Regulatory Research

17            Institute (“NRRI”) at the Ohio State University and later as the Manager of Regulatory

18            Policy & Market Analysis with the Regulatory Operations Staff of the Nevada Public

19            Utilities Commission. As a consultant, I have served a variety of clients including

20            government agencies, utility customers, and utility companies. I have served as an expert

21            witness and/or advisor in over 150 rate cases and rulemakings of various types. I have

22            written testimony filed in the following utility regulatory commission jurisdictions:

23            Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Idaho, Kansas, Kentucky,


     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank          Case No. 25-00079-UT                                 Page 3
  1           Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma,

 2           South Carolina, Texas, Wyoming, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. At

 3           NMSU, I direct a professional Graduate Certificate Program in Public Utility Regulation

 4           & Economics, a Masters of Economics program, and help deliver nationally-recognized

 5           rate case training programs endorsed by the National Association of Regulatory Utility

 6           Commissioners (“NARUC”) and attended by hundreds of regulatory professionals from

 7           across the United States. My resume is attached as Exhibit LB-1.

 8    Q.     ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING?

 9    A.     I am testifying on behalf of the Utility Division Staff (“Staff”) of the New Mexico Public

10           Regulation Commission (“Commission” or “PRC”).

11    Q.     HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY WRITTEN TESTIMONY IN PUBLIC UTILITY

12           REGULATORY PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO COMMISSION?

13    A.     Yes, I have provided testimony in several proceedings before the Commission.


14 II.     PURPOSE AND SUMMARY


15    Q.     WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

16    A.     I was asked by Staff to provide independent analysis and recommendations regarding

17           Southwestern Public Service Company’s (“SPS” or “Company”) proposed cost allocation

18           and rate design within their pending rate case before the Commission.

19    Q.     PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS.

20    A.     The following summarizes my review and recommendations.

21           1.     The SPS-proposed jurisdictional allocation used to separate the revenue

22                  requirement between the Texas, New Mexico, and Federal Energy Regulatory

23                  Commission (“FERC”) jurisdictions utilizes forecasted 12-CP and energy


      Direct Testimony of Larry Blank       Case No. 25-00079-UT                                Page 4
  1                 allocation ratios and this methodology is not used in those other jurisdictions. This

 2                 creates a mismatch that causes the potential for over- or under-recovery of revenue

 3                 requirement. Because SPS has forecasted much more load growth in New Mexico

 4                 than in Texas, and the fact that Texas does not allow forecasted test years, causes

 5                 some double recovery of revenue requirement if these different methods are

 6                 applied. Texas requires the use of actual historical data and allows adjustments for

 7                 known and measurable changes but does not allow forecasts. My recommendation,

 8                 solely for the purpose of the jurisdictional separations, is to use what is required

 9                 and allowed in Texas. This will maintain consistency on this important matter to

10                 avoid over- or under-recovery of revenue requirement.

11          2.     It is imperative that when any capacity and/or energy facility costs are directly

12                 assigned to New Mexico that there be an offsetting credit in the jurisdictional

13                 allocation factors. The Cunningham BESS only provides capacity value and no

14                 energy value. Therefore, for the purposes of this rate case, I am recommending an

15                 offsetting adjustment to the New Mexico 12-CPs equal to the expected accredited

16                 capacity of the storage system. This reduces the amount of the remaining capacity

17                 costs that is allocated to New Mexico.

18          3.     The level of revenue requirement increase recommended by Staff is much lower

19                 than that proposed by SPS.       This allows more latitude or bandwidth in the

20                 distribution of the revenue increase across the customer classes. I recommend that

21                 no rate class receive an increase less than 50% of the Staff’s system average base

22                 rate revenue increase. I recommend that the above-cost revenue from those rate

23                 classes set at 50% of the system average be allocated to the other rate classes in




     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank        Case No. 25-00079-UT                                 Page 5
  1                 proportion to the cost-based increases of those classes. This establishes Staff’s

 2                 proposed banding in which no customer class receives less than 50% of system

 3                 average, and most of the other classes, including residential, range between 150%

 4                 to 200% of system average. Only one rate class, Secondary General Service, would

 5                 receive an increase at cost of service.

 6          4.     I recommend limiting the service availability charge for residential customers to

 7                 $15.00 per month, which is a 33.9% increase over the current charge of $11.20, and

 8                 consistent with the percentage increase for small general service.

 9          5.     The large proposed increases in the reactive power charges may be of concern, and

10                 these increases have been somewhat mitigated in Staff’s proposed rates.

11          6.     I recommend approval of the Company’s proposed reductions in the seasonal rate

12                 differentials and the time-of-use on-peak and off-peak rate differentials. These

13                 changes are supported by system reliability and cost considerations.

14          7.     The Company’s proposed on-peak time period, summer days 1pm to 8pm seems

15                 reasonable.

16          8.     The implementation of a new demand ratchet for primary general service and a

17                 significant change in the ratchet for transmission service customers draws questions

18                 of appropriate timing for implementation. As proposed, these ratchets would

19                 retroactively consider the billing demands from the previous 11 months in the first

20                 month the ratchet becomes effective. The Commission should consider a phase-in

21                 period of 11 months before the ratchets take effect. That is, in the 12th billing cycle

22                 after the rates take effect, SPS will now start using the higher of the current month’s

23                 billing demand or 85% of the past 11 months.




     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank        Case No. 25-00079-UT                                   Page 6
  1               9.     Staff generally supports the Company’s proposed Electric Affordability Program

 2                      (“EAP”). Because this program is being implemented for the first time, this benefit

 3                      is in addition to the LIHEAP support already received by these customers, and not

 4                      knowing the revenue impact on other customers, I recommend that the PIPP be

 5                      based on five percent (5%) of household income and not the three percent proposed

 6                      by the Company.

 7        Q.     HOW DOES STAFF’S CASE SUPPORT AFFORDABILITY FOR RESIDENTIAL

 8               AND SMALL GENERAL SERVICE CUSTOMERS?

 9                      First, Staff’s direct testimony results in a substantial reduction in the revenue

10               deficiency, from the proposed $175.4 million down to $47.7 million, which is a large

11               decrease in the SPS’ proposed revenue requirement increase. Second, Staff’s banding

12               recommendation serves to mitigate the increases to residential and small general service

13               customers. Third, Staff’s general support of the SPS-proposed EAP will directly address

14               affordability concerns for some low-income customers.

15                      Average bill impacts for Residential and Residential Heating under Staff’s

16               recommended rates are 6.3% and 6.9%, respectively. By comparison, the Company’s

17               proposed rates for Residential and Residential Heating produce bill impacts of 23.5% and

18               22.2%, respectively.

19 III.        JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION RATIOS DESERVE ATTENTION

20        Q.     HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION RATIOS

21               PROPOSED BY SPS TO SEPARATE COSTS BETWEEN TEXAS, NEW MEXICO,

22               AND FERC WHOLESALE?




          Direct Testimony of Larry Blank       Case No. 25-00079-UT                                Page 7
  1   A.         Yes. These are sponsored by SPS Witness Taylor J. Hurt. 1

 2   Q.         ARE THERE IMPORTANT CONSIDERATIONS IN THE SELECTION OF THE

 3              JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION RATIOS?

 4   A.         Yes. The allocation ratios should be based on a reasonably acceptable methodology and

 5              consistently applied in all three jurisdictions. As stated by Mr. Hurt: “In addition, because

 6              SPS is a multi-jurisdictional utility, the method of determining cost responsibility across

 7              those jurisdictions must be consistent so that the combination of costs applicable to each

 8              jurisdiction is not under- or overstated.” 2

 9   Q.         WHAT ALLOCATION RATIOS DOES MR. HURT DEVELOP FOR THE

10              PURPOSE           OF       SEPARATING          COSTS     BETWEEN          THE      THREE

11              JURISDICTIONS?

12   A.         He utilizes forecasted 12-CPs to develop allocation ratios for production and transmission

13              capacity related costs.       For production energy costs, he develops forecasted energy

14              consumption ratios for each jurisdiction.

15   Q.         DO      YOU      HAVE        ANY    CONCERNS        WITH      THE     JURISDICTIONAL

16              ALLOCATION METHODS USED BY SPS IN THIS CASE?

17   A.         Because the forecasted demand and energy increases in New Mexico are substantially

18              larger than those for Texas, the use of forecasted 12-CPs and energy to calculate the

19              jurisdictional allocation ratios causes the New Mexico allocation ratios to be much higher

20              than base test year. This may be acceptable if there was a high level of confidence in the

21              accuracy of the forecasts and if Texas and the FERC allowed and followed the same

22              jurisdictional allocation methodology. Texas does not allow a forecasted test year and


     1
         See Hurt Direct Testimony at pp. 6-13.
     2

     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank               Case No. 25-00079-UT                               Page 8
  1          requires a 12-month historical test year with allowed adjustments for known and

 2          measurable changes. The FERC requires the use of historical FERC Form 1 data that feed

 3          into the approved formula rate setting mechanism. Because Texas does not allow a

 4          forecasted test year, the concern is that the use of forecasted 12-CPs and energy in New

 5          Mexico causes a mismatch between Texas and New Mexico, and as Mr. Hurt has testified,

 6          there is a risk of under- or over-stated revenue requirement. This mismatch in

 7          methodologies is substantial and should be a concern to the Commission.

 8   Q.     IN THIS CASE, DOES THE MISMATCH IN JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION

 9          CAUSE AN UNDER-STATEMENT OR OVER-STATEMENT OF REVENUE

10          REQUIREMENT?

11   A.     Because New Mexico’s forecasted demand increases are significantly higher than Texas’s,

12          using different allocation methods would result in an overstatement and over-recovery of

13          the revenue requirement if a Texas rate case were pending. This is because the Texas

14          allocation ratios proposed in the New Mexico case are smaller than the ratios that would

15          be used in an actual Texas rate case. As a result, a portion of the same revenue requirement

16          would be recovered twice across the two jurisdictions.

17   Q.     DO YOU HAVE A RECOMMENDATION TO REMEDY THIS CONCERN?

18   A.     Yes. It is very important that the methods used in each jurisdiction are completely

19          consistent for the purpose of allocating the revenue requirement between the jurisdictions.

20          Therefore, SPS should be required in this New Mexico case to use the same jurisdictional

21          allocation methodology as used in Texas, which is a 12-month historical period with

22          adjustments only for known and measurable changes. Given the data available in this case,

23          I recommend using the 12-CPs and energy as developed by SPS for the base year, not the




     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank        Case No. 25-00079-UT                                 Page 9
  1          future test year, to calculate the jurisdictional allocation ratios for the sole purpose of

 2          separating the revenue requirement between the Texas, New Mexico, and the FERC

 3          wholesale jurisdictions. SPS is free to propose adjustments to this base year for any

 4          missing known and measurable changes, consistent with what is allowed by the Texas

 5          PUC, as part of its rebuttal case.

 6   Q.     HOW LARGE ARE THE DIFFERENCES IN FORECASTED DEMAND

 7          GROWTH BETWEEN TEXAS AND NEW MEXICO IN THE APPLICATION?

 8   A.     For 12-CP production demand, SPS projects an increase of 524 MW in production demand

 9          for New Mexico, but only 174 MW for Texas. For 12-CP transmission demand, SPS

10          projects an increase of 569 MW for New Mexico, but only 203 MW for Texas.

11   Q.     DO YOU HAVE ANY OTHER ADJUSTMENTS TO THE 12-CP NEW MEXICO

12          AND TEXAS JURISDICTIONAL LOADS WHEN USING THE BASE PERIOD TO

13          CALCULATE JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION?

14   A.     Yes, I have two. First, because SPS is losing 100 MW of wholesale production contract

15          demand. I have removed that 100 MW of wholesale demand from the production 12-CP

16          jurisdictional allocation to New Mexico. Second, because SPS is directly assigning all of

17          the Cunningham BESS cost to New Mexico, Staff recommends that New Mexico receive

18          all of the accredited capacity benefit from that BESS. SPS estimates the accredited

19          capacity of the Cunningham BESS to be about 24 MW. This capacity should be credited

20          to the New Mexico 12-CPs used to allocate the remaining production capacity. Therefore,

21          I have reduced the New Mexico 12-CPs by 24 MW. The SPS-forecasted New Mexico

22          average production 12-CP of 2,236 MW has been reduced by 524 MW by using the base




     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank         Case No. 25-00079-UT                              Page 10
  1          year and another 24 MW downward adjustment for the Cunningham BESS for a revised

 2          12-CP of 1, 1,688 MW.

 3   Q.     IS IT FAIR, JUST AND REASONABLE TO DIRECTLY ASSIGN BESS COSTS TO

 4          NEW MEXICO BUT NOT RECOGNIZE THE BESS CAPACITY IN THE

 5          ALLOCATION OF OTHER SYSTEM PRODUCTION CAPACITY?

 6   A.     No. The BESS capacity assigned to New Mexico reduces reliance on the remaining system

 7          production capacity by the same amount. It is unfair to also include that capacity value in

 8          the allocation of the remaining system capacity. Therefore, my recommendation to adjust

 9          the 12-CP allocation based on the Cunningham accredited capacity paid by New Mexico

10          is fair, just and reasonable.

11   Q.     WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION FOR ANY CAPACITY IN WHICH THE

12          COSTS ARE DIRECTLY ASSIGNED TO NEW MEXICO?

13   A.     It is imperative that when any capacity and/or energy facility costs are directly assigned to

14          New Mexico that there be an offsetting credit in the jurisdictional allocation factors. The

15          Cunningham BESS only provides capacity value and no energy value. Therefore, for the

16          purposes of this rate case, I am recommending an offsetting adjustment to the New Mexico

17          12-CPs equal to the expected accredited capacity of the storage system. This reduces the

18          amount of the remaining capacity costs that is allocated to New Mexico. Future projects

19          that potentially may be directly assigned to New Mexico may have both capacity and

20          energy benefits. Such capacity and energy values must offset the amount of remaining

21          capacity and energy that is allocated between Texas and New Mexico. For purposes of the

22          Commission's decision in this case, I recommend the following: Direct assignment of the

23          costs of the Cunninham BESS to New Mexico requires capacity credit in the calculation




     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank         Case No. 25-00079-UT                                Page 11
  1          of the 12-CP jurisdictional allocation ratio applied to the remaining system production

 2          capacity. The expected accredited capacity for Cunningham BESS is 24 MW and the New

 3          Mexico 12-CPs shall be reduced by that amount. Future projects that may provide both

 4          capacity and energy with costs directly assigned to New Mexico must also cause an energy

 5          adjustment in the jurisdictional allocations of remaining energy resources.

 6   Q.     DOES      YOUR       RECOMMENDATION                FOR      THE      JURISDICTIONAL

 7          ALLOCATION RATIOS DIFFER SIGNIFICANTLY FROM THOSE PROPOSED

 8          BY SPS?

 9   A.     Yes.   Table 1, below, provides the adjusted base period 12-CP averages for each

12          were to accept Staff’s recommendation for jurisdictional allocation it would result in a

13          $56.7 million reduction in revenue deficiency. However, this is subject to change if SPS

14          provides adjustments to the base year consistent with the Texas methodology allowing

15          known and measurable changes.

2   Q.     DO YOU THINK SPS SHOULD PURSUE YOUR SUGGESTIONS AND USE

3          THEIR REBUTTAL CASE TO UPDATE THE BASE YEAR LOAD DATA WITH

4          ANY MISSING KNOWN AND MEASURABLE CHANGES CONSISTENT WITH

5          THE REQUIREMENTS IN TEXAS?




    Direct Testimony of Larry Blank        Case No. 25-00079-UT                              Page 13
  1    A.        Yes. The Company’s use of forecasted numbers for the development of the jurisdictional

 2              allocation ratios is inconsistent with Texas and with FERC. Because Texas does not allow

 3              a forecasted test year, the only way to make New Mexico and Texas consistent is by using

 4              a base year with adjustments for known and measurable changes including weather

 5              normalized load data. My recommendation to use the Texas methodology for the test year

 6              only pertains to the development of the jurisdictional allocation ratios to ensure consistency

 7              in that step. My recommendation does not affect SPS’ proposed future test year for other

 8              steps in developing the New Mexico revenue requirement.


 9 IV.        CLASS COST OF SERVICE AND REVENUE INCREASE DISTRIBUTION

10    Q.        HAVE YOU REVIEWED SPS’ CLASS COST OF SERVICE STUDY?

11    A.        Yes. This study is sponsored by SPS witness Taylor J. Hurt.

12    Q.        DO YOU HAVE ANY RECOMMENDED CHANGES TO THE COST STUDY

13              SPONSORED BY MR. HURT?

14       A.     No. For future rate cases, I recommend that the system load factor used to weight average

15              demand in the average and excess demand allocation method be calculated using the single

16              system peak demand, rather than the four-month average system peak used to compute the

17              excess demands. If the system load factor is calculated using the same demand measure as

18              the excess demands, then the average and excess demand method becomes the same as the

19              4-CP method, which is a special case of average and excess demand.

20    Q.        HAS SPS ENTERED INTO A STIPULATION TO ENGAGE STAKEHOLDERS IN

21              REVIEWING COST ALLOCATION METHODS?

22    A.        Yes. On April 10, 2026, SPS entered into a stipulation agreement in Case No. 25-00085-

23              UT, in which it will “convene a working group to engage stakeholders and Staff to evaluate


      Direct Testimony of Larry Blank            Case No. 25-00079-UT                                 Page 14
  1          and analyze alternatives to SPS’s current retail customer class cost allocation for both demand

 2          (capacity) and energy costs. The results of this analysis will be presented in SPS’s next rate

 3          case.” This will be an opportunity to begin consideration of alternative allocation methods in

 4          order to provide New Mexico with additional capacity credit for SPS’s system renewable

 5          resources that are paid by New Mexico customers 100%.

 6   Q.     HAS STAFF UPDATED THE CLASS COST OF SERVICE STUDY TO REFLECT

 7          STAFF’S RECOMMENDED REVENUE REQUIREMENT?

 8   A.     Yes. The SPS class cost of service study has only been updated to reflect Staff’s

 9          recommended revenue requirement and the electronic version can be made available for

10          review by the Commission and parties.

11   Q.     HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE COMPANY’S PROPOSAL FOR REVENUE

12          INCREASE DISTRIBUTION TO MITIGATE RATEPAYER IMPACTS?

13   A.     Yes. This proposal is sponsored and explained by SPS witness Alexander G. Trowbridge

14          pp. 14-17. Their proposal uses a range from 100% to 150% of the rate increase to total

15          revenue for guidance. This proposal is similar to the banding that is often considered in

16          New Mexico rate cases to mitigate increases to rate classes that would otherwise receive

17          very high increases at cost of service. However, SPS uses percent of total revenue rather

18          than base rate revenue to guide their gradualism proposal.

19   Q.     ARE STAFF’S BANDING RECOMMENDATIONS IN PART DEPENDENT ON

20          THE OVERALL INCREASE UNDER CONSIDERATION?

21   A.     Yes. For example, Staff’s proposed revenue increase is substantially less than that proposed

22          by SPS, which provides for more latitude (or bandwidth) in considering banding options.

23          In addition. Staff’s banding recommendations are intended to result in affordable rates that

24          are fair, just and reasonable.

  1 V.     RATE DESIGN

 2   Q.     HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE RATE DESIGN PROPOSALS MADE BY THE

 3          COMPANY?

 4   A.     Yes. These are sponsored by SPS witness Alexander G. Trowbridge.

 5   Q.     ARE YOU RECOMMENDING ANY CHANGES TO THE COMPANY’S

 6          PROPOSED RATE DESIGN?

 7   A.     The Company’s proposed increase to the Residential Service Availability Charge or

 8          “customer charge” is very significant. Based upon the public interest for rates to be

 9          affordable and fair, just and reasonable, I recommend limiting the increase to 33.9%, which

10          is $15.00. The current charge is $11.20. This is the only change from the Company’s

11          proposed rate design.

12   Q.     ARE YOU SPONSORING STAFF’S RECOMMENDED RATES?

13   A.     Yes. Staff’s recommended rates are provided in the attached Exhibit LB-3.

14   Q.     WERE THERE ANY OTHER RATE DESIGN PROPOSALS THAT MAY BE OF

15          CONCERN?

16   A.     Another potential concern was SPS’ proposed large increases in the reactive power charges

17          for the Secondary, Primary, and Transmission General Service classes. These proposed

18          increases were over 1000%. With Staff’s proposed revenue requirement, these have been

19          mitigated within my recommended rates without changing the Company’s rate design

20          model. However, the Commission should be aware that these increases in the reactive

21          power charges are still very large increases.

22   Q.     DID SPS PROPOSE ANY RATE DESIGN CHANGES THAT ARE AN

23          IMPROVEMENT IN YOUR OPINION?




     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank        Case No. 25-00079-UT                               Page 18
  1   A.         Yes. SPS has proposed to somewhat decrease the differential in seasonal rates and to

 2              significantly decrease the differential between on-peak and off-peak rates. I agree with

 3              these proposed changes.

 4   Q.         WHY DO YOU AGREE WITH REDUCING THE DIFFERENTIAL BETWEEN

 5              SUMMER RATES AND NON-SUMMER RATES?

 6   A.         As more emphasis has been placed on system reliability and resource adequacy during the

 7              winter months, closing the differential between the higher summer rates and the lower

 8              winter rates makes sense from a system reliability perspective and cost of resource

 9              adequacy viewpoint. 3

10   Q.         WHY DO YOU AGREE WITH REDUCING THE DIFFERENTIAL BETWEEN
